5.4  
MEDICAL FEES FOR COURT ATTENDANCES AND PREPARATION  
BEST PRACTICE GUIDELINES ISSUED BY THE LAW SOCIETY OF SINGAPORE AND THE SINGAPORE MEDICAL ASSOCIATION (March 2006)  

5.4.1  
These Guidelines are issued jointly by the Law Society of Singapore and the Singapore Medical Association. They are intended to provide guidance to lawyers and medical practitioners as to what is “reasonable” in dealings between lawyers and medical practitioners in relation to fees for court attendances and preparation of reports. These Guidelines have been prepared in the spirit of mutual respect of the professionalism, the independence and the integrity of the legal and medical professions. The Guidelines apply only to fees charged for court attendances and preparation of reports.  

5.4.2  
These Guidelines only affect the conduct of civil litigation. In particular, the Guidelines do not bind counsel or medical practitioners in criminal proceedings or in the assessment of the fees of counsel. The Guidelines do not apply to fees charged for attendance at a Coroner’s Court or at an inquest. The Guidelines do not apply to fees charged for attendance at a disciplinary tribunal or other professional disciplinary proceedings.  

5.4.21  
It is recognised that the preparation of a report and attendance at court may be time-consuming and may require considerable effort. The fees charged should be reasonable and commensurate with the time and effort involved.  

5.4.22  
It is not appropriate for a medical practitioner to charge a fee for attendance at court if the attendance is for the purpose of giving evidence in a case in which the practitioner has treated the patient.  

5.4.23  
If the medical practitioner is required to attend court to give evidence in a case in which the practitioner has not treated the patient, the practitioner may charge a fee for attendance at court and preparation of a report. The fee should be reasonable and commensurate with the time and effort involved.  

5.4.24  
In practice, a personal injury case, the evidence of both the plaintiff and the defendant’s medical experts is usually required. The plaintiff’s medical expert is usually the treating doctor. The defendant’s medical expert is usually an independent medical expert. The defendant’s medical expert may be required to attend court to give evidence. The defendant’s medical expert may charge a fee for attendance at court and preparation of a report.  

5.4.3  
It is important that the medical practitioner should not charge a fee for attendance at court if the attendance is for the purpose of giving evidence in a case in which the practitioner has treated the patient.  

5.4.4  
Appointments at a doctor’s office are like appointments on the private and public health care systems. If a doctor is unable to keep an appointment, the doctor should notify the patient as soon as possible and arrange for another appointment. If a doctor is unable to keep an appointment, the doctor should notify the patient as soon as possible and arrange for another appointment. If a doctor is unable to keep an appointment, the doctor should notify the patient as soon as possible and arrange for another appointment.  

Notes:  
(1) A “Professional Witness” is called only because of his direct doctor-patient relationship with the plaintiff.  
(2) “Expert Witness” is called or appointed for a “second opinion” or expert testimony in legal proceedings. It is not a doctor-patient relationship.  
(3) An expert witness who is a plaintiff’s medical doctor and who gives expert testimony in legal proceedings is a “Professional Witness”. If the case is subsequently postponed it is subject to the same scale of fees as the “Expert Witness”.  
(4) The court attendance fee that applies if the case is subsequently postponed is subject to the same scale of fees as the “Expert Witness”.  
(5) The above amounts are negotiable between the practitioner and the Counsel.  
(6) The above amounts are negotiable between the practitioner and the Counsel.  
(7) One day is equivalent to 8 hours.
